BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: The brief high pressure ridge over the area will quickly break down by Wednesday afternoon, as a closed Pacific upper low steers into the lower northwest and Great Basin.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Slightly warmer temperatures and dry conditions expected over most areas today.
- Light valley rain and mountain snow this evening in southeast Oregon, moving into southwest Idaho by Monday morning.
- Cooler and unsettled pattern continuing throughout the coming week, with valley rain and mountain snow expected through Friday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Breezy and dry conditions will continue for most areas this morning, with the southwest ID side seeing temperatures a few degrees above normal today as high pressure remains over the area. A slow-moving cold front, accompanied by a band of precipitation, will steer eastward across eastern OR this morning through early Monday, and then through southwest ID early Monday through Tuesday. Valley rain showers and mountain snow are expected with this frontal passage today through early Tuesday, before tapering off east by late Tuesday. Total rain accumulations for the valleys will remain on the lower side between 0.15-0.35 inches from today through late Tuesday, with amounts greater than 0.30 inches concentrated along the eastern OR side. Snow levels will stay between 5500-6500 feet MSL today through Monday, dropping off to 4500-5500 by Monday night. As such, higher elevation areas will see light snow accumulations today through Tuesday. For now, high mountain peaks are expected to see 4 to 9 inches of total snow by late Tuesday. The frontal passage will return a gradual cooling trend Monday through Tuesday. Following the frontal passage, a brief ridge of high pressure will return over the area late Tuesday through early Wednesday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The brief high pressure ridge over the area will quickly break down by Wednesday afternoon, as a closed Pacific upper low steers into the lower northwest and Great Basin. This system will bring a more prolonged precipitation event from Wednesday through the end of the week. Guidance continues to suggest the core of the low digging south of our area, steering abundant wraparound moisture and continuous precipitation over our area through late Friday. Continuous valley rain showers and mountain snow are expected Wednesday through late Friday. Lower valley areas are tentatively looking at around 0.20 inches of total rainfall. Latest long-range guidance has snow levels hanging in the 3500-4500 ft range through Saturday. Valleys can see a rain/snow mix, mainly on Friday. Higher mountain peaks can still see possible snow accumulations of 5 to 10 inches total by early Saturday. Not much cooling is expected with this system, and temperatures are expected to hang near or slightly below seasonal normals through Friday. Come early Saturday, the system will steer out of our area as a ridge builds back in. Saturday and Sunday will generally see slightly warmer temperatures and relatively drier conditions. Another Pacific trough is projected to steer into the region, but considerable uncertainty remains over its precipitation timing and intensity. For now, late Saturday through early Sunday will see slight chances of precipitation mainly over higher terrain areas.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Unfortunately for snow lovers, both global ensembles and deterministic runs have trended downward in snow amounts with the system for next weekend. What was previously a potent cutoff low is now being depicted as a much weaker, open trough.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Areas of fog again this morning, including the northern I-25 corridor and I-70 corridor.
- A return to mild and dry conditions Sunday through Tuesday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Fog has been slow to make progress in the last couple of hours, with observations showing an area of fog over Lincoln County, and another area of fog spilling over the CO-WY border over northernmost Weld County. At this time, a Dense Fog Advisory remains in effect for Lincoln County until 10 am Sunday morning. Visibilities could drop to <1/4 mile at times in the advisory area and adjacent plains. The advisory may need to be expanded if dense fog develops elsewhere. While we still expect fog to increase in coverage closer to sunrise, low clouds may limit the duration and extent of the lower (<1/4 mi) visibilities.

How much temperatures warm up Sunday afternoon will be heavily dependent on the erosion (or lack thereof) of fog and/or low clouds. Given the trends in model guidance and was has been observed over the last couple of days, fog may be slow to erode over the southeastern portion of our CWA, with scattered low clouds lingering into the afternoon. As such, high temperatures over areas affected by the stubborn low clouds (mainly Lincoln County) may run 5-10 degrees cooler than areas with direct sunshine Sunday afternoon. Residual moisture west of the Continental Divide may also lead to low clouds persisting through the late morning for our western counties.

An upper level ridge to our west will continue to strengthen and drift east over our area on Monday, bringing us temperatures that are about 10 degrees warmer than climatology. Afternoon temperatures on Monday and Tuesday will climb into the low 60s for the Denver metro and east CO plains, with most mountain valleys warming up into the 50s each day as well. Flow aloft turns southerly and strengthens ahead of the next system on Tuesday afternoon, although the strongest winds now appear to remain just east of our area.

A weakening shortwave move over Colorado on Wednesday, and this will be our next chance for precipitation. As the previous AFD stated, this shortwave will move rather quick, only allowing for a few hours of light snow showers at the high elevations. Given the quick nature of this system, only a trace of snow accumulation is expected, with amounts up to 1-2 inches at the highest peaks >12kft. Cross-barrier westerly flow aloft on the backside of this disturbance will also encourage a period of downsloping winds late Wednesday morning. Wind gusts up to 35 mph could be possible for mountains valleys, with gusts as high as 55 mph for ridgelines and areas above the tree line. At low elevations, a cold front will push through the northern Colorado plains and Denver metro sometime late Wednesday with breezy northerly winds behind it. Slightly cooler temperatures should arrive behind this cold front, although temperatures are still likely to remain a couple of degrees above average.

Unfortunately for snow lovers, both global ensembles and deterministic runs have trended downward in snow amounts with the system for next weekend. What was previously a potent cutoff low is now being depicted as a much weaker, open trough. This weaker solution would only suggest light mountain snow at best Friday into the weekend. However, it is worth noting that some ensemble members still bring at least one inch of snow to the Denver metro sometime next weekend. One possible reason for the whiplash in solutions seems to be that global models keep struggling with the location of cyclogenesis upstream off the northern Pacific Coast. As has become evident over the last few days, there is a considerable uncertainty in the forecast beyond day 4, and the forecast could still shift in either direction. Decent agreement still exists in temperatures cooling down to seasonal averages for the weekend.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Seasonal temperatures will stick around on Thursday with little to no weather impacts expected. Some lingering breezy conditions are still likely west of the Laramie Range on Thursday, but the rest of the forecast area will see a quiet day.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Areas of fog will continue into Sunday morning. A Dense Fog Advisory remains in effect until 900 AM MST for areas along and east of the I-25 corridor, including the Cheyenne Ridge in the southern Nebraska Panhandle.
- A slightly more active pattern is expected into the middle of next week, with low precipitation chances returning Wednesday into Thursday.

- Strong gusty winds are looking more likely for late Tuesday night and Wednesday for the Wind Prone areas of southeast Wyoming. Windy conditions expected elsewhere as a cold front moves into the high plains.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Current KCYS radar loop shows the sprinkles and flurries last night dissipating early this morning as the poorly organized Pacific storm system redevelops over the Texas and Oklahoma panhandle...with any remaining energy with the northern portion of the shortwave trough dissipating as well. Fog is still observed across the high plains, mainly along the I-25 corridor and the Cheyenne Ridge as it extends eastward into Kimball and Sidney Nebraska. Otherwise, some light drizzle is possible in this area, but should brief and end well before sunrise. Surface winds are already starting to shift into the southwest over Cheyenne with increasing winds out of the southwest expected for the I-25 corridor from 100 AM to sunrise. Fog and low CIGS will gradually lift with low clouds and fog remaining over the Nebraska Panhandle and far eastern Wyoming until mid morning. Kept the Dense Fog Advisory out for now, but may need to tweak the areal coverage with fog expected to lift along I-25. Will continue to monitor and adjust as need this morning.

For today and Monday, models show lingering morning cloud cover early Sunday before give way to mostly sunny skies by the afternoon with high temperatures trending back into the 50s to low 60s. Portions of the western Nebraska Panhandle will likely remain in the low 50s due to lingering low clouds. Even warmer for Monday as a Pacific shortwave ridge axis translates eastward into the Intermountain West and amplifies over the Front Range Monday morning. Surface winds will remain out of the south as the ridge axis moves into the Front Range, which is enough low level upslope to hold onto some low clouds, and possibly fog, Sunday night over Box Butte, Morrill, and Cheyenne Counties. Further west, should be enough of a westerly wind component and dry air intrusion to prevent fog development. Added some fog into early Monday morning from Sidney to Alliance. Otherwise, pleasant mid-November day expected with highs in the upper 50s to mid 60s.

All models show the next Pacific storm system rapidly moving onshore, producing rainfall as far south as southern Calif and mountain/Great Basin snowfall Tuesday. This will be our next weather maker which is forecast to impact the region late Tuesday and Wednesday. As of right now, models are not indicating a closed storm system and still show an open wave trough ejecting northeast over Wyoming and Montana. This storm track favors mountains snow, cooler temperatures, and windy conditions across southeast Wyoming (strong winds possible across the wind prone areas). Will continue to monitor this system over the next few days.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The majority of the long term will feature relatively benign weather with a return to more seasonable temperatures and breezy conditions.

A pattern change will arrive on Wednesday as a trough swings into the Rockies. A cold front will move across the area, late Tuesday night or early Wednesday morning, leading to high temperatures in the 40s and 50s--roughly average for this time of year. This front will be mostly dry, with predominately west winds promoting a dry downslope environment. The mountains, however, could see a quick shot of snow, with the Sierra Madre Range picking up a few inches of accumulation. The Snowys will likely be shadowed and not see much in the way of accumulations. The bigger concern with the frontal passage will be strong winds. Marginal high winds will be possible as MSLP gradients compress from the front. Winds aloft will increase up to about 50 kts with decent subsidence, so cannot rule out 60 MPH gusts during the day in the typical southeast Wyoming wind prones.

Seasonal temperatures will stick around on Thursday with little to no weather impacts expected. Some lingering breezy conditions are still likely west of the Laramie Range on Thursday, but the rest of the forecast area will see a quiet day. Friday into the weekend, things could get interesting with a potential impactful winter storm. Of course, its still over a week away with plenty of time for models to come to a solution, but there is a chance for accumulating snow and windy conditions.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Forecast models continue to show another system arriving late this week on Friday and Saturday. Models still show an open wave setup, so as a result the precipitation amounts continue to decrease.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry and mild conditions Sunday and Monday with morning fog possible.
- The next system will bring valley rain and mountain snow on Tuesday and Wednesday, followed closely by another storm system on Friday and Saturday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: There is potential for fog and low stratus once again tonight. The only difference is that clouds moving in form the west could prohibit some of that development.

Our focus then shifts to another shortwave trough moving through the area from Tuesday afternoon through Wednesday. While this system will be slightly cooler, the bulk of the precipitation is still expected to fall ahead of the cold front. As a result, snowfall totals should look similar to the previous system, peaking at 4-8" in the southern mountains, with lighter amounts farther north. Snow levels will also be hovering around 7-9 kft. Behind the front, temperatures will drop to near or slightly below normal for much of the week.

Forecast models continue to show another system arriving late this week on Friday and Saturday. Models still show an open wave setup, so as a result the precipitation amounts continue to decrease. There is still some differences among the models with regards to strength and timing, so confidence is not high attm. Most of the moisture is expected to arrive ahead of the cold front, making timing critical. Snow levels could drop to some valley floors Friday night into Saturday morning. For now, however, the specifics remain uncertain.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: For Thursday through Sunday, operational models and ensemble mean data continue to trend further north and not as deep with the next eastern Pacific system digging across the Great Basin and lifting out across the Northern Rockies.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Areas of dense fog across portions of the southeast Plains and into the San Luis Valley through the morning, keeping temperatures cool through the day.
- More low clouds and patchy fog across the plains later tonight into Monday morning.
- Quick moving system to bring snow to areas along and west of the ContDvd Tuesday and Tuesday night, with breezy downslope flow keeping warm and dry conditions across the plains.
- Another passing system to bring unsettled weather to the higher terrain of the ContDvd later Thursday and Friday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Current water vapor imagery and upper air analysis has broad upper trough translating across the Rockies with a weak circulation evident across the western Texas and Oklahoma Panhandle at this time. Said weak upper low is keeping some showers rotating across the plains late this evening, with generally light upslope flow keeping stratus and dense fog across the plains, especially across El Paso County, at this time.

For today and tonight, the Rockies broad upper trough and Western Panhandle low continue to translate east, with weak north to northwest flow aloft in place across the region through Sunday night. Movement of the weak upper low will continue to rotate a few showers across the far southeast plains through the early morning hours, with light moist low level upslope flow remaining across southeast Colorado as well. This will keep areas of fog, locally dense, through the early morning hours, with stratus expected to slowly clear from west to east through mid morning and into the early afternoon. With that said, we will keep the current Dense Fog Advisory in place for El Paso County through 9 am. Later shifts may need to expand it further south and east across the plains and possibly for portions of the San Luis Valley, if mid and upper level clouds clear faster than anticipated, or there is not enough mixing with the passing showers across the plains to help prevent dense fog development.

The slow decrease in stratus and fog will keep temperatures on the cool side Sunday, with highs in the mid to upper 40s expected across the plains, and in mainly in the 40s and 50s across the higher terrain, save for 30s at the peaks. With persistent weak low level upslope flow, latest model data indicates stratus and patchy fog redeveloping across the plains Sunday night, with expected overnight lows in the 20s and 30s areawide.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Weak west to northwest flow aloft transitions to more southwest through the day Monday, ahead of our next weather maker digging across the West Coast. Dry weather remains on tap for Monday, with patchy fog and stratus diminishing through the morning across the plains, as some high level waa clouds spreads in from west to east across the area through the afternoon. High temperatures also warm slightly into the 50s across the plains and mainly 40s and 50s across the higher terrain. The slow increase in southwest flow helps to develop lee troughing across the plains Monday night, with lows in the 20s and 30s once again across the region, warmest in the banana belt, with developing westerly flow will keep temperatures up overnight.

For Tuesday and Wednesday, latest operational models and ensemble data are in good agreement of increasing southwest flow aloft through the day Tuesday, as the West Coast upper trough translates across the Intermountain West and Great Basin. This will start to bring some moisture into the Continental Divide with increasing chances of precipitation through the day. Moderate west to southwest flow across the region Tuesday night into Wednesday as said broad trough continues to translate east across the Rockies and into the high plains, will keep the best precipitation coverage across the higher terrain, mainly along and west of the Continental Divide Tuesday night, with precipitation diminishing behind the passing system through the day Wednesday. The quick movement of the system will limit precipitation totals, with the potential for low end advisory snow amounts possible, mainly across the eastern San Juan mountains.

The increased downslope and mixing will help boost temperatures back above seasonal levels in the 60s across the plains both Tuesday and Wednesday, with the potential for stronger westerly winds in the lee of the eastern mountains Tuesday night into early Wednesday morning.

For Thursday through Sunday, operational models and ensemble mean data continue to trend further north and not as deep with the next eastern Pacific system digging across the Great Basin and lifting out across the Northern Rockies. This will keep the best chances of precipitation once again along and west of the Continental Divide Thursday night through Friday night, with moderate to strong westerly flow keeping generally warm, dry and breezy conditions in place across the eastern Plains. Moderate north to northwest flow behind the passing system to keep slightly cooler and mainly day conditions across the region for Saturday and Sunday.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Behind the cold front passage late Tuesday, precipitation gradually tapers off through early Wednesday, drying out briefly ahead of yet another storm expected to impact our area on Thursday into Friday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Patchy fog will dissipate this morning across northern Utah valleys and near Evanston, WY.

- A cold, Pacific system will impact the region later Monday into Wednesday morning. Accumulating snow will impact most Utah mountain locations as well as the Wasatch Back. Expect the heaviest totals across the upper Cottonwoods and southern Mountains.
- Another colder Pacific system will impact the region Thursday into early Saturday. Snow levels will lower to near to below 5000 feet by Saturday morning.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Clearing skies behind today's cold front will make for quite the crisp night across Utah and southwest Wyoming, with some of the coldest low temperatures of the season so far. Many lower elevation valleys will see temperatures dip into the low to mid 30s, except the low 40s across lower Washington County. Given recent rainfall and clearing skies tonight, there is a 20% chance for fog-prone areas across the Cache Valley and Wasatch Back to see freezing fog develop overnight. The limiting factor will be how quickly a deck of high clouds moves into the region, as these clouds could limit radiational cooling overnight.

High pressure builds in across the Intermountain West on Sunday into Monday, keeping conditions dry and mild through this period. This pattern will be brief, as another system is slated to impact the region on Tuesday. This next system looks quite similar that of today's: a fast-moving negatively tilted trough swinging through the Great Basin, bringing widespread rain and mountain snow ahead of a cold front. As such, likely looking at similar impacts with this upcoming storm. H7 temperatures around -4 to -5C indicate snow levels as low as 7000 feet, though best chances for accumulating snowfall will generally be above 8000-9000 feet. Current forecast calls for snowfall amounts between 3 to 8 inches for most mountains above 8000 feet, except locally up to 10 inches for the southern mountains.

Behind the cold front passage late Tuesday, precipitation gradually tapers off through early Wednesday, drying out briefly ahead of yet another storm expected to impact our area on Thursday into Friday. There is more considerable uncertainty regarding this late-week storm, as models struggle to converge on the track and magnitude of the associated closed low. While this system is likely to bring another round of widespread precipitation, the uncertainty lies in the precipitation accumulations and just how cold of an airmass this storm brings to the region. Current H7 temperature spread late Thursday is between -3 to -9C, with the latter supportive of snow down to valley levels. This scenario is still on the lower end, with around 20% of models resolving this colder airmass, but still something to keep an eye on as we get closer.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: You could trigger an avalanche where you find more than 10 inches of new, dense snow forming a slab over weak snow on steep, shady slopes above treeline.

Watch for cracking or collapsing in the new snow, as these are clear warning signs that a slab has formed. Safer travel conditions can be found on lower-angled slopes and at lower elevations where less new snow fell.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: A few inches of new snow late on Saturday won't be enough to raise avalanche concerns. Most slopes don't have enough snow for avalanches and are safe for travel. At high elevations, steer around isolated spots of firm, drifted snow below ridges or in steep gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has yet to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. Except on the steepest, highest-elevation, north-facing slopes, the mountains are snow-free. Avalanches will be unlikely until a deeper, layered snowpack builds. Once winter does arrive, even a small amount of snow with enough wind can create unstable avalanche conditions. If you're traveling in the mountains during or after a storm, be wary of steep, wind-loaded features at upper elevations and watch out for terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information as more snow accumulates
hazard_discussion: Due to a warm and dry fall season, the mountains in our forecast zones remain mostly dry, with little to no snow on the ground. As you're waiting for winter to arrive and the mountain snowpack to stack up, here are a few things to consider:
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Avalanche conditions are generally safe. If you are at high elevations and observe more than about 6 inches of new or wind-drifted snow, or see shooting cracks, steer around steep terrain features.
